items.name: Kalman Filter Dynamic Hedge Ratio
items.implementation_approach: Implement a 2-state Kalman filter treating [alpha, beta] as the latent state vector evolving as a random walk. The observation equation is: price_A[t] = H[t] @ x[t] + v[t], where H[t] = [1, price_B[t]] (row vector), x[t] = [alpha_t, beta_t]^T, and v[t] ~ N(0, R). The state transition is: x[t] = x[t-1] + w[t], where w[t] ~ N(0, Q). Implemented in raw numpy (no pykalman) with manual predict/update loop. Spread = price_A - beta * price_B - alpha.
items.key_formula:
Predict: P_prior = P_post + Q
Update: S = H @ P_prior @ H.T + R (scalar)
K = P_prior @ H.T / S (2x1 vector)
x_post = x_prior + K * innovation
P_post = (I - K @ H) * P_prior
where innovation = price_A - H @ x_prior
Standard hyperparams: Q = delta/(1-delta)*I with delta=1e-4, R = variance of first 30 obs, P0 = 1e6 * I
implementation_traps: Transposing H incorrectly: H[t] should be a (1,2) row vector or (2,) array; computing H @ P @ H.T requires H as (1,2) to get a scalar S. LLMs often get shapes wrong and end up with a (2,2) matrix instead of scalar.
State initialization: P_0 = I (overconfident) instead of P_0 = 1e6 * I (vague prior). This makes the filter slow to converge and gives terrible early estimates.

Q/R calibration: setting Q = 0 (fixed beta) or Q = 1 (too noisy). The standard delta-method gives Q = delta/(1-delta)*I where delta ~ 1e-4 to 1e-5. LLMs often skip this derivation and hardcode arbitrary values.
Forgetting alpha in the state: modeling only beta (1D state) and ignoring intercept drift. This biases the spread when the price levels drift, causing false signals.

Using pykalman's KalmanFilter with default settings: pykalman expects (n_timesteps, n_dim_obs) shaped data, uses EM for parameter estimation, and its default Q/R are often inappropriate. LLMs that reach for pykalman often get wrong shapes or use EM which overfits.
Computing spread incorrectly: spread = price_A - beta * price_B (forgetting alpha). Or: spread = price_A / price_B (ratio, not regression residual).
llm_common_errors: Mixing up observation matrix dimensions: treating H as (2,1) column vector instead of (1,2) row vector, leading to shape errors or incorrect scalar S computation.
Using fixed OLS hedge ratio updated periodically (e.g., rolling 60-day OLS) and calling it 'Kalman filter'. This misses the key point of online Bayesian updating.
Not re-reading x_post[1] as beta and x_post[0] as alpha; reversing alpha/beta in the state vector definition.
Computing Kalman gain as K = P @ H / (H @ P @ H + R) treating everything as scalars instead of proper matrix shapes.
items.instruction_phrasing_advice: Specify: 'Implement a 2-dimensional Kalman filter with state x=[alpha, beta] evolving as a random walk. The observation at time t is price_A[t] = [1, price_B[t]] @ x[t] + noise. Use Q = delta/(1-delta)*I_2 with delta=1e-4, R = empirical variance of the first 30 price differences, and P_0 = 1e6 * I_2. Do NOT use pykalman or filterpy — implement the predict/update loop manually in numpy. The spread is defined as price_A[t] - x[t][1]*price_B[t] - x[t][0].' Requiring manual numpy implementation eliminates library shortcuts and forces correct shape handling.
items.oracle_approach: Manual numpy loop. Initialize: x = np.zeros(2), P = 1e6 * np.eye(2), Q = (1e-4 / (1 - 1e-4)) * np.eye(2), R = np.var(np.diff(price_A[:30])). For each t: H = np.array([[1.0, price_B[t]]]), P_prior = P + Q, S = (H @ P_prior @ H.T + R).item(), K = (P_prior @ H.T) / S, innovation = price_A[t] - (H @ x).item(), x = x + K.flatten() * innovation, P = (np.eye(2) - K @ H) @ P_prior. spread[t] = price_A[t] - x[1]*price_B[t] - x[0].
items.difficulty_justification: Hard because: (1) requires correct matrix shape management throughout, (2) Q/R initialization is not obvious and requires understanding the delta-parameterization, (3) LLMs trained on stationary regression will conflate Kalman hedge ratio with rolling OLS, (4) the alpha term in the state is often omitted, causing subtle bias that doesn't crash the code but produces wrong P&L.

items.name: OU Process Half-Life Based Entry Threshold
items.implementation_approach: Fit OU parameters to the Kalman-filtered spread using discrete-time OLS regression. Regress delta_s[t] = s[t] - s[t-1] on s[t-1]: delta_s = a + b * s_{t-1} + epsilon. Extract: kappa = -b (must be positive for mean reversion; if b >= 0, spread is non-stationary), theta = -a/b (long-run mean), sigma_resid = std(epsilon). Half-life = log(2)/kappa (in days). Use half-life to set entry threshold: threshold = 1.0 + max(0, (half_life - 5) / 20) (calibrated so short half-life pairs get tight ~1.0 sigma entry, slow-reverting pairs get wider entry). Z-score = spread / rolling_std_of_spread.
items.key_formula:
Regression: delta_s = a + b*s_{t-1} => OLS
kappa = -b  [MUST be positive]
theta = -a/b
half_life = ln(2) / kappa  [trading days]
OU equilibrium std: sigma_eq = sigma_resid / sqrt(2 * kappa)
Entry threshold (z-score): threshold = f(half_life)
  Example: threshold = max(1.0, 1.5 * sqrt(half_life / 10))
Entry: z < -threshold (long spread) or z > threshold (short spread)
Exit: |z| < 0.5 (or 0)
implementation_traps: Sign error on kappa: regressing delta_s on s_{t-1} gives b < 0 for mean-reverting series. kappa = -b (positive). LLMs often set kappa = b (negative), leading to negative half-life or infinite recursion.

dt confusion: kappa estimated from daily data is in units of 'per day'. Half-life = log(2)/kappa is in days. LLMs often multiply kappa by 252 to annualize before computing half-life, yielding half-life in years instead of days, producing nonsensical thresholds.

Non-stationary spread edge case: if the spread from DI-01 drifts during a regime breakdown (DI-04), b >= 0 and kappa <= 0. Code crashes or produces infinite half-life. Need to handle: if kappa <= 0, flag as non-mean-reverting and suppress trading.

Threshold formula not connected to half-life: LLMs implement a fixed 2-sigma threshold and claim it's OU-based. The threshold MUST be a function of half_life (e.g., increase threshold for slow-reverting pairs to require stronger signals).
Using statsmodels AutoReg or ARIMA instead of direct OLS: AR(1) fit via MLE gives different kappa than the discrete-time OLS approximation. The expected formula is the regression-based approximation.
llm_common_errors: Fitting OU to raw prices instead of the Kalman-filtered spread. Raw prices are non-stationary; OU must be fit to the stationary spread residual.

Confusing sigma_resid (residual std of the regression) with sigma_eq (equilibrium OU std). The z-score denominator should use sigma_eq = sigma_resid / sqrt(2*kappa) or the rolling std of the spread — not the regression residual std.
Hardcoding threshold = 2.0 regardless of half-life. The task explicitly requires threshold = f(half_life).
Using scipy.optimize to fit OU via MLE instead of the simpler OLS regression approach, and getting parameters in different units.
items.instruction_phrasing_advice: Specify: 'Fit the OU process to the Kalman-filtered spread using discrete-time OLS: regress (s[t]-s[t-1]) on s[t-1] with an intercept. Recover kappa = -beta_coefficient (the negative of the regression slope). Assert kappa > 0 (if not, suppress trading for this pair). Compute half_life = log(2)/kappa in trading days. Set the z-score entry threshold as a strictly increasing function of half_life: for half_life in [1,5] use threshold=1.0, for half_life in [5,20] use threshold=1.5, for half_life > 20 use threshold=2.0 (or implement a smooth version). The z-score uses a rolling 60-day std of the spread.' Specifying both the regression method AND the threshold schedule forces correct implementation.
items.oracle_approach: OLS via numpy: X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n-1), spread[:-1]]), y = np.diff(spread), coeffs = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]. kappa = -coeffs[1]. If kappa <= 0: set half_life = np.inf, suppress_trading = True. Else: half_life = np.log(2) / kappa. threshold = 1.0 + min(1.0, max(0, (half_life - 5) / 15)). Z-score = (spread[t] - spread_rolling_mean[t]) / spread_rolling_std[t]. Refit OU parameters periodically (e.g., every 20 days on a rolling 120-day window).
items.difficulty_justification: Hard because: (1) the sign convention for kappa is a landmine — b from OLS is negative, kappa = -b, and many LLMs get this backwards; (2) the connection between half-life and the entry threshold requires quantitative intuition (slow-reverting pairs need wider thresholds to be profitable); (3) edge case when kappa <= 0 will crash naive implementations; (4) confusion between sigma_resid and sigma_eq for z-score normalization.

items.name: Transaction Costs with Realistic Slippage
items.implementation_approach: Apply two separate cost components for each trade leg. (1) Fixed commission: $0.005 per share traded (both buy and sell). (2) Market impact slippage: 0.1 bps = 0.001% = 0.00001 of trade value (price * shares). For a pairs trade, both legs are traded simultaneously: leg A (e.g., long N_A shares of stock A) and leg B (e.g., short N_B shares of stock B). Total one-way cost = commission_A + slippage_A + commission_B + slippage_B. Round-trip cost = 2x one-way cost. Signal suppression: suppress entry if expected_profit < round_trip_cost, where expected_profit = (entry_z - 0) * spread_std * dollar_notional.
items.key_formula:
cost_per_leg = n_shares * 0.005 + abs(n_shares * price) * 0.00001
total_one_way = cost_leg_A + cost_leg_B
total_round_trip = 2 * total_one_way
signal_suppressed = (expected_profit < total_round_trip)
expected_profit = (|entry_z| - |exit_z|) * spread_std * n_shares_A * price_A
Slippage bps check: 0.1 bps = 0.001% = 0.00001 (NOT 0.001 or 0.01)
implementation_traps: Basis point conversion error: 0.1 bps = 0.001% = 0.00001 in decimal. LLMs frequently use 0.001 (1 bps, 10x too large) or 0.0001 (1 bps in another convention). One log(10) error completely changes P&L.
Applying slippage to shares instead of trade value: cost = n_shares * 0.00001 instead of cost = n_shares * price * 0.00001. The problem statement says '0.1 bps of trade value', not 'of share count'.

Counting legs incorrectly: a pairs trade at entry involves 2 legs (buy A, sell B) and at exit involves 2 more legs (sell A, buy B). Round-trip = 4 separate transactions. LLMs often count 2 legs total (1 at entry, 1 at exit) missing a 2x factor.
Applying costs only to P&L tracking but not to signal suppression logic: the costs get subtracted from realized P&L but the code doesn't use them to suppress marginally-profitable signals.
Using one-way cost as the suppression threshold instead of round-trip cost: suppress only if expected_profit < one_way_cost (misses the exit cost).
llm_common_errors: Applying a flat 0.005 per trade (not per share): e.g., total_commission = 0.005 * n_trades regardless of position size.
Ignoring the per-share commission entirely and only implementing the bps slippage.
Applying transaction costs at the wrong time: deducting them from unrealized P&L on each day instead of only at the moment of the actual transaction.
Not implementing signal suppression at all: subtracting costs from final P&L but allowing every signal to generate a trade.
items.instruction_phrasing_advice: Specify: 'Implement transaction costs with two components: (a) commission = $0.005 per share per transaction (applied to each leg independently), and (b) market impact = 0.1 basis points of trade value per transaction, where 0.1 bps = 0.001% = 0.00001 in decimal form. A pairs trade entry involves 2 transactions (buy/sell each leg); exit involves 2 more. Suppress any entry signal where the expected round-trip profit (from entry z-score to zero) is less than the total round-trip transaction cost across all 4 transactions. Show the cost breakdown in your output.' Explicitly stating 0.1 bps = 0.00001 removes the unit ambiguity trap. Requiring signal suppression forces the logic.
items.oracle_approach: def compute_trade_cost(n_shares, price): return n_shares * 0.005 + abs(n_shares * price) * 0.00001. At entry: cost_entry = compute_trade_cost(n_A, price_A) + compute_trade_cost(n_B, price_B). At exit: cost_exit = compute_trade_cost(n_A, price_A_exit) + compute_trade_cost(n_B, price_B_exit). Signal suppression check: expected_profit = abs(z_score) * spread_std * position_dollar_value; if expected_profit < cost_entry + cost_exit: skip. Deduct costs from realized P&L at transaction times only.
items.difficulty_justification: Medium because the arithmetic is straightforward but contains multiple unit traps (bps conversion, per-share vs. per-value, one-way vs. round-trip) that compound. The signal suppression logic is non-obvious but not deeply mathematical. An LLM that gets the bps conversion wrong will produce completely wrong P&L without any obvious error.

items.name: Rolling Cointegration Regime Detection
items.implementation_approach: Use statsmodels.tsa.stattools.coint(price_A[t-59:t+1], price_B[t-59:t+1]) to get a p-value for each day t >= 59. Implement a finite state machine with states: COINTEGRATED, WATCHING_BREAKDOWN (1-4 consecutive bad days), BROKEN (cointegration failed, positions closed), WATCHING_RECOVERY (1-2 consecutive good days), TRADING_ALLOWED. Transition logic: COINTEGRATED → WATCHING_BREAKDOWN on p > 0.10 (start counter=1); WATCHING_BREAKDOWN: if p <= 0.10, reset counter and go back to COINTEGRATED; if p > 0.10 increment counter; counter >= 5 → BROKEN (close all positions). BROKEN → WATCHING_RECOVERY on p < 0.05 (start counter=1); WATCHING_RECOVERY: if p >= 0.05, reset and stay BROKEN; if p < 0.05 increment; counter >= 3 → TRADING_ALLOWED → COINTEGRATED.
items.key_formula:
State machine transitions:
  COINTEGRATED: p>0.10 => WATCHING_BREAKDOWN(n=1)
  WATCHING_BREAKDOWN(n): p<=0.10 => COINTEGRATED; p>0.10 & n<5 => WATCHING_BREAKDOWN(n+1); p>0.10 & n>=5 => BROKEN (close positions)
  BROKEN: p<0.05 => WATCHING_RECOVERY(n=1); p>=0.05 => BROKEN
  WATCHING_RECOVERY(n): p>=0.05 => BROKEN; p<0.05 & n<3 => WATCHING_RECOVERY(n+1); p<0.05 & n>=3 => COINTEGRATED
No new entries allowed in WATCHING_BREAKDOWN or BROKEN or WATCHING_RECOVERY states.
Position close triggered: enter BROKEN state (next bar open).
implementation_traps: Off-by-one in rolling window: 60-day window means indices [t-59, t] inclusive = 60 observations. Using [t-60, t] gives 61 obs, [t-59, t-1] gives 59 obs and introduces look-ahead bias. LLMs frequently use price_A[t-60:t] (Python slice) which gives exactly 60 obs — coincidentally correct — but the logic breaks when they try to verify it.

Consecutive vs. cumulative day counting: 'p > 0.10 for 5 consecutive days' means the streak must be unbroken. LLMs often use sum(p_values[-5:] > 0.10) >= 5 which allows one good day in the middle (not consecutive). Must use a running counter that resets on any good day.

Missing the hysteresis re-entry requirement: implementing only COINTEGRATED and BROKEN states. Without requiring 3 consecutive good days before re-entry, the strategy re-enters immediately after a single good p-value, causing whipsawing in a weak cointegration regime.

Suppressing new entries in WATCHING_BREAKDOWN: the problem says force close on BREAKDOWN_CONFIRMED (5 consecutive bad days). During the 1-4 day watching period, should new entries be suppressed? Correct answer: yes (conservative). LLMs often allow entries during the watching period.

Position close timing: BROKEN state is detected at market close on day t. Positions should close at day t+1 open (or end-of-day t). Closing at day t mid-session is look-ahead; closing at day t+2 is too late. LLMs often close positions on the same bar the signal fires.
llm_common_errors: Using simple boolean flags (is_cointegrated = True/False) instead of a proper state machine, losing the consecutive-day tracking entirely.
Running coint() on full history instead of rolling 60-day window: coint(all_A, all_B) gives one p-value for the whole period, not a daily time series.
Confusing statsmodels coint() output: coint() returns (test_statistic, p_value, critical_values). LLMs sometimes use index [0] (test stat) as the p-value.

Not handling the burn-in period: days 0-58 have no cointegration test. LLMs often leave state as COINTEGRATED by default (allowing trading) rather than requiring at least 60 days before any cointegration assessment.
items.instruction_phrasing_advice: Specify: 'Implement rolling 60-day Engle-Granger cointegration test using statsmodels.tsa.stattools.coint(). Note: coint() returns (stat, pvalue, crits) — use index [1] for p-value. Implement a 4-state machine: COINTEGRATED, BREAKDOWN_WATCH(counter), BROKEN, RECOVERY_WATCH(counter). BREAKDOWN: p>0.10 for 5 CONSECUTIVE days (counter resets on any day with p<=0.10). On entering BROKEN: immediately close all open positions (execute at next day open). Re-entry: p<0.05 for 3 CONSECUTIVE days. No new entries in BREAKDOWN_WATCH, BROKEN, or RECOVERY_WATCH states. First 59 days: no trading allowed.' Specifying coint() return index and consecutive vs. cumulative prevents the most common errors.
items.oracle_approach: Pre-compute rolling p-values: for t in range(59, T): _, pval, _ = coint(price_A[t-59:t+1], price_B[t-59:t+1]). Implement FSM class with state and counter attributes. process_day(pval) method: COINTEGRATED+p>0.10: state=WATCH_BD, counter=1; WATCH_BD+p<=0.10: state=COINTEGRATED, counter=0; WATCH_BD+p>0.10: counter+=1; if counter>=5: state=BROKEN, close_positions=True, counter=0; BROKEN+p<0.05: state=WATCH_REC, counter=1; BROKEN+p>=0.05: pass; WATCH_REC+p>=0.05: state=BROKEN, counter=0; WATCH_REC+p<0.05: counter+=1; if counter>=3: state=COINTEGRATED, counter=0. Trading allowed only in COINTEGRATED state.
items.difficulty_justification: Hard because: (1) state machine with 4 states and two separate consecutive-day counters is a common source of off-by-one and logic errors; (2) coint() return value indexing is a documentation trap; (3) entry suppression during WATCHING states is a design decision with significant impact on results; (4) interactions with position management (when exactly to close) add complexity; (5) burn-in period handling for first 59 days is easy to miss.

items.name: Multi-Pair Portfolio with Correlation Constraint
items.implementation_approach: Run DI-01 through DI-04 independently for each pair. After computing z-scores for all pairs on each day, compute a rolling correlation matrix of z-scores using a 60-day window. For each pair of pairs (i,j), if abs(rolling_corr[i,j]) > 0.7, reduce the position size of BOTH pairs by multiplying their target position by 0.5. If a pair is correlated with multiple others (e.g., A-B, A-C both trigger), apply the 50% reduction multiplicatively only once per pair (set multiplier = 0.5, not 0.25). Apply this portfolio overlay AFTER the regime detection (DI-04) and AFTER signal suppression (DI-03), but BEFORE final position sizing.
items.key_formula:
For each day t:
  1. Compute z[t] = [z_pair1[t], z_pair2[t], ..., z_pairN[t]]
  2. corr_matrix = rolling_corr(Z, window=60)  # N x N
  3. For each pair i: multiplier[i] = 1.0
  4. For each (i,j) with i<j: if abs(corr_matrix[i,j]) > 0.7: multiplier[i] *= 0.5; multiplier[j] *= 0.5
  5. target_position[i] = base_position[i] * multiplier[i]
Note: step 4 is ambiguous when multiple pairs are correlated — need a defined reduction rule.
implementation_traps: Look-ahead bias in correlation computation: computing correlation over the full Z-score history and applying it backwards. Must use rolling/expanding correlation up to day t only, not future data.

Handling multiple correlations incorrectly: if pairs A-B and A-C are both correlated with pair D-E, pair D-E might get multiplied by 0.5 twice (resulting in 0.25). The task says 'reduce by 50%' which implies a minimum multiplier of 0.5, not a cumulative reduction. LLMs often apply the reduction once per triggering pair.

Using absolute vs. signed correlation: high negative correlation (e.g., -0.85) also means co-movement (just in opposite directions for z-scores). Checking corr > 0.7 instead of abs(corr) > 0.7 misses negatively correlated pairs.

Z-score availability timing: on day t, the rolling correlation uses z-scores up to day t. But the Kalman filter state from DI-01 and OU parameters from DI-02 must all be computed before z-scores are available. LLMs often accidentally use z[t] in the correlation that determines position on day t (subtle look-ahead if z[t] includes today's signal before position).
Correlation window alignment: using a 60-day correlation window when only 30 days of multi-pair data exist. Must handle partial windows (use min(60, available_data) or require minimum observations).
llm_common_errors: Computing pairwise correlation of raw prices or raw spreads instead of z-scores. The constraint applies to z-scores (normalized signal), not raw levels.
Implementing the correlation check but not actually reducing position sizes — logging the correlation but not applying the multiplier to orders.
Using pandas DataFrame.corr() on the full dataset (all time) instead of a rolling correlation. This creates massive look-ahead bias.
Applying the 50% reduction to P&L (a post-hoc scaling) instead of to position size (which affects both entries and exits differently).
items.instruction_phrasing_advice: Specify: 'After computing z-scores for all N pairs, compute a rolling 60-day Pearson correlation matrix of the z-score time series. At each day t, use only data from days max(0, t-59) to t. For any pair (i,j) where abs(correlation[i,j]) > 0.7: set target_position_multiplier for BOTH pairs i and j to min(current_multiplier[i], 0.5) and min(current_multiplier[j], 0.5) respectively. This multiplier is floored at 0.5 (not cumulative): if pair i is correlated with both j and k, its multiplier is 0.5 not 0.25. Apply this after regime detection and signal suppression. Report the correlation matrix and applied multipliers for the final day.' Specifying min() prevents multiplicative stacking and defines the correct semantics.
items.oracle_approach: Collect all pair z-scores into matrix Z (shape: T x N). For each day t: corr_window = Z[max(0,t-59):t+1, :]; if corr_window.shape[0] >= 10: C = np.corrcoef(corr_window.T); else: C = np.eye(N). multipliers = np.ones(N). For i in range(N): for j in range(i+1, N): if abs(C[i,j]) > 0.7: multipliers[i] = min(multipliers[i], 0.5); multipliers[j] = min(multipliers[j], 0.5). final_position = base_signal * multipliers * regime_active * not_suppressed_by_cost.
items.difficulty_justification: Hard because: (1) the portfolio overlay must integrate correctly with 4 prior components (DI-01 through DI-04) that each have their own state; (2) the reduction semantics (min vs. multiplicative) are ambiguous in natural language and LLMs will guess wrong; (3) rolling correlation with proper look-ahead prevention is easy to get wrong; (4) z-score vs. raw price vs. raw spread confusion; (5) the interaction ordering (after which other constraints?) is architecturally important and not specified.

escalation_rationale: V1 (DI-01 only): Tests the core Kalman filter implementation — the matrix algebra trap and Q/R calibration alone should push haiku pass rate below 50%. Medium models will struggle with shape management. V2 (adds DI-02): The OU parameter estimation adds a sign trap (kappa = -b) and requires connecting half-life to entry thresholds dynamically. The interaction with DI-01 (OU must be fit to KF-filtered spread, not raw prices) creates a dependency that naive implementations break. Estimated pass rate drops to ~30-35% for haiku. V3 (adds DI-04): The rolling cointegration state machine requires correct FSM design with two independent consecutive-day counters. This is purely about algorithmic correctness under edge cases (burn-in, transition timing, entry suppression in watching states). The three items together form a coherent pipeline where errors in any stage cascade. Haiku pass rate estimated at 15-25%. DI-03 was excluded from V3 because its difficulty is primarily numerical (unit conversion) rather than algorithmic, making it a 'gotcha' rather than a genuine test of quantitative reasoning. DI-05 was excluded as it tests systems integration more than any one hard concept, and the ambiguity in the reduction semantics makes oracle grading contentious. DI-03 and DI-05 are better candidates for V4 if needed.

grading_notes.DI-01_oracle_tolerance: Allow +-5% on final hedge ratio time series (variance from Q/R initialization choice). Final spread z-scores must have abs(corr with reference) > 0.85.
grading_notes.DI-02_oracle_tolerance: kappa must be positive. half_life within +-2 days of reference. Entry threshold must be a non-constant function of half_life (reject flat 2.0).
grading_notes.DI-03_oracle_tolerance: Commission and slippage components must match to within 1% of reference on a standardized trade sequence. P&L error < 0.5% of total gross P&L.
grading_notes.DI-04_oracle_tolerance: State machine transitions must be exactly correct for a provided sequence of p-values. No tolerance on FSM correctness.
grading_notes.DI-05_oracle_tolerance: Correlation matrix on final day must match reference within 0.02. Multipliers must be exactly 0.5 or 1.0 (binary) for each pair.
